title: Rep. Meredith Craig voted yea on HB251, a drone and law enforcement and aviation facilities bill
text:
Rep. Meredith Craig voted yea on HB251, a drone and law enforcement and aviation facilities bill
A. C. Howard
Rep. Meredith Craig (R-77th) voted yea on HB251, a bill on drone law enforcement and aviation facilities that passed the Ohio House 89-5 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and include interpretation to clarify its provisions.
The bill amends Ohio’s aeronautics law to explicitly cover heliports, vertiports, spaceports and seaplane bases and sets rules for law enforcement use of unmanned aerial vehicles. It requires police to obtain a search warrant before using a drone to enter or observe the interior of a house or place when a warrant would be required for an in-person search, and it generally makes warrantless surveillance data inadmissible in criminal cases. The bill permits warrantless drone use in defined circumstances, including near national borders, during emergencies, for traffic enforcement and crash scenes, and for research. It bars law enforcement from deploying armed drones, limits private drone surveillance of individuals without consent, requires documentation and retention of flight and surveillance data, gives criminal defendants access to surveillance data about them, and classifies flight data as a public record subject to exemptions.
HB251 was introduced by Bernard Willis.
Craig is serving in her first term as State Representative for Ohio House District 77, which includes all of Wayne County. She previously worked in the Ohio Senate through the Legislative Service Commission fellowship and served as senior legislative aide to Representative Ron Amstutz. Craig holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in History and Political Science from Malone University and graduated from the Jo Ann Davidson Leadership Institute in 2015. Her background also includes roles in the Kasich and DeWine administrations and advocacy work with the Ohio Chamber of Commerce.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
